title: Вика расстаётся с Нагиевым  (Vika Breaks Up with Nagiyev)

segments.t: After Chef Barinov reassures Max that nothing happened with Katya, Vika arrives at Nagiyev's apartment and finds his ex-wife Kristina hiding in the wardrobe. Listen to the full conversation in Russian first.
Держи лимон, чтобы не заболеть.
У вас с Катей ничего не было.
Ну и супер, я очень рад.
Дима, это я, ты дома?
Дима, где ты прячешься?
Привет, в целом как твои дела?
Дима, мы с тобой расстаёмся.
Надеюсь, в данной конкретной ситуации ты не против?
В данной конкретной ситуации, видимо, нет.
Свои вещи я лучше завтра соберу.
Думаю, да, сегодня всем будет неловко.
Прощай, Дмитрий Владимирович.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
Держи лимон, чтобы не заболеть.
'Take this lemon so you do not get sick.' In Russian, the idea of 'hold' flows naturally into 'to get sick' without extra filler words.
У вас с Катей ничего не было.
'Nothing happened between you and Katya.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'at' and finishing on 'was'.
Ну и супер, я очень рад.
'Well that is great, I am very glad.' The meaning hinges on 'come on' working together with 'glad' in spoken Russian.
Дима, это я, ты дома?
'Dima, it is me, are you home?' Notice how Russian expresses 'Dima' and 'at home' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
Дима, где ты прячешься?
'Dima, where are you hiding?' Vika addresses the listener with the informal singular 'you' alongside 'are hiding'. Dmitry Nagiyev answers right away.
Привет, в целом как твои дела?
'Hi, how are things with you overall?' Notice how Russian expresses 'hello' and 'things to do' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
Дима, мы с тобой расстаёмся.
'Dima, you and I are breaking up.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'Dima' before landing on 'are breaking up'.
Надеюсь, в данной конкретной ситуации ты не против?
'I hope in this particular situation you do not mind?' Notice the reflexive suffix on the verb meaning 'hope', turning the action back on the subject. Dmitry Nagiyev answers right away.
В данной конкретной ситуации, видимо, нет.
'In this particular situation, apparently not.' Dmitry Nagiyev anchors the line on 'this', while 'no' completes the thought.
Свои вещи я лучше завтра соберу.
'I had better pack my things tomorrow.' The grammar packs 'one's own' and 'to collect' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
Думаю, да, сегодня всем будет неловко.
'I think so, today it would be awkward for everyone.' The meaning hinges on 'think' working together with 'awkward' in spoken Russian. Vika answers right away.
Прощай, Дмитрий Владимирович.

'Farewell, Dmitry Vladimirovich.' In Russian, the idea of 'farewell' flows naturally into 'Vladimirovich' without extra filler words. Alright, let's hear the entire conversation one more time from start to finish.

Catching Kristina in Nagiyev's closet makes Vika's decision effortless. In the next scene, Kristina steps out of the closet as Nagiyev tries to control his temper.
